title: Synergistic targeting of senolytic and senomorphic action with dual-engineered biomimetic macrophage nanovesicles for mitigating osteoarthritis

sections.abstract:
Osteoarthritis (OA), a leading cause of chronic disability worldwide, is increasingly recognized to be driven by the accumulation of senescent chondrocytes (sCDs) and their deleterious pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Existing therapies, including senolytics and senomorphics, lack cell-specific targeting and fail to neutralize the heterogeneous components of SASP. Here, we develop a dual-engineered macrophage membrane camouflaged, self-assembled nanoplatform (BS@MD) that combines senolytic and senomorphic functions synergistically. Within the OA microenvironment, BS@MD acts as a “nanosponge” to broadly neutralize SASP through overexpressed cytokine receptors derived from LPS-primed macrophage membranes. This process alleviates chondrocyte senescence and facilitates the phenotypic shift of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory M2 state. Additionally, surface conjugation with an anti-DPP4 antibody enables BS@MD to selectively target sCDs and disassemble in the acidic lysosomal environment, releasing bortezomib (BTZ) and sabutoclax (Sab). These agents act synergistically to inhibit the NF-κB and BCL-2 pathways, thereby inducing sCDs apoptosis and suppressing SASP production, effectively disrupting the senescence-inflammation feedback loop. In the anterior cruciate ligament transection (ACLT)-induced OA mouse model and naturally aged OA mouse model, BS@MD enhances joint retention, reduces cartilage degradation and inflammation, and promotes cartilage homeostasis. Overall, this work pioneers a dual-pronged senotherapeutic strategy for non-surgical OA management.

Keywords: Engineered nanovesicles, Osteoarthritis, Senescent chondrocytes elimination, SASP neutralization, DPP4 targeting
sections.introduction:
Osteoarthritis (OA) is a major contributor to chronic disability worldwide, especially in aging populations, and imposes a growing socioeconomic burden due to the lack of effective disease-modifying therapies [ 1 ]. OA progression involves multi-factor such as obesity, joint injury, and genetics, with cellular senescence now recognized as a key pathological driver [ 2 ]. Recent studies have identified senescent chondrocytes (sCDs) in OA cartilage [ 3 , 4 ]. These cells not only lose their capacity to maintain cartilage homeostasis but also secrete pro-inflammatory and catabolic factors—collectively referred to as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), these factors propagate secondary senescence in surrounding cells and accelerate joint degeneration [ 5 ]. Although senolytic therapies show promise in aging-related diseases, they face major challenges: limited cell specificity, efficacy restricted to certain senescent subtypes, and inability to neutralize the complex and heterogeneous SASP components (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β). These limitations underscore the need for strategies that both selectively eliminate sCDs and broadly suppress SASP to effectively halt OA progression and restore joint function.

Mechanistically, sCDs’ survival and SASP secretion are regulated by two key pathways: the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family and the pro-inflammatory NF-κB signaling [ 6 ]. In senescent cells, elevated BCL-2 proteins (e.g., BCL-xL, BCL-w) prevent apoptosis by binding to the BH3 motifs of pro-apoptotic proteins (e.g., BAX or BAK) through conserved molecular interactions. BH3 mimetics, such as Navitoclax, block these interactions to promote senescent cell clearance [ 7 ]. Concurrently, DNA damage-induced NF-κB activation drives chronic inflammation and SASP production, further accelerating OA pathology [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. Although pharmacological inhibitors of BCL-2 and NF-κB have shown efficacy in reducing senescent cells and SASP, systemic delivery often causes off-target toxicity, and monotherapy fails to address both apoptosis resistance and SASP heterogeneity. These challenges highlight the need for spatiotemporally controlled dual-targeting strategies that can selectively suppress both pathways in sCDs while sparing healthy tissue.

In recent years, carrier-free self-assembled nanomedicines—based on supramolecular interactions for co-loading multiple therapeutics—have emerged as promising tools to enhance drug stability and synergistic efficacy [ 11 ]. Compared to traditional nanocarriers, these systems offer advantages such as simple preparation, high drug loading, and an “all-in-one” delivery platform. However, challenges such as poor colloidal stability, rapid clearance, and lack of active targeting have hindered clinical translation [ 12 ]. To address these limitations, external modification strategies have been explored, notably cell membrane-mimicking nanoplatforms. Due to the retention of the antigen spectrum from the parent cell, cell membrane-mimicking nanoplatforms enable immune evasion, prolonged circulation, targeted delivery, and pro-inflammatory cytokine neutralization. Various biomimetic systems—derived from tumor cells, white blood cells, red blood cells, platelets, and macrophages, have been developed. Among them, macrophage membranes exhibit strong inflammatory tropism and cytokine interception, with validated applications in diseases like atherosclerosis [ 13 ], periodontitis [ 14 ], and OA [ 15 ]. Leveraging macrophage membrane-camouflaged nanovesicles for inflammation-targeted delivery and SASP neutralization offers a novel therapeutic paradigm in OA management.

Targeting sCDs specifically is essential to minimize off-target effects. However, conventional senescence markers, including p16 INK4a , p21, and senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) are intracellular, limiting their utility in targeted delivery. Recently, the discovery of surface markers such as DPP4, a serine protease expressed on senescent WI-38 fibroblasts and chondrocytes [ 16 , 17 ], provides a viable solution for selective targeting. Compared to normal cells, DPP4 is significantly overexpressed on the surface of senescent cells, especially sCDs, which provides great potential for precisely targeting sCDs from the outside.

Here, we developed a biomimetic macrophage nanovesicle integrating senolytic and senomorphic activities into a unified platform ( Fig. 1 ). A carrier-free nanosystem (BS) was self-assembled by co-loading bortezomib (BTZ) and sabutoclax (Sab). BTZ, a clinically approved proteasome inhibitor, suppresses NF-κB signaling by preventing IκB degradation, thereby reducing SASP production and pro-inflammatory cytokine release [ 18 ]. Sab is a pan-BCL-2 family inhibitor, which promotes apoptosis of sCDs by antagonizing anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-2, BCL-xL, and MCL-1 [ 19 ]. The combination of BTZ and Sab thus provides a dual senotherapeutic strategy, simultaneously attenuating SASP-driven inflammation and selectively eliminating senescent cells. To enable targeted delivery, BS was cloaked with engineered macrophage membranes functionalized with anti-DPP4 antibodies (BS@MD). These membranes facilitate SASP neutralization via decoy cytokine receptors (IL-6Rα, TNFR1, IL-1R1), while the anti-DPP4 antibody guarantees specific binding to sCDs. Once internalized, BS disassembles in the acidic lysosomal environment, releasing drugs that synergistically induce sCDs apoptosis and suppress SASP. In the anterior cruciate ligament transection (ACLT)-induced OA mouse model and naturally aged OA mouse model, BS@MD effectively eliminated sCDs, reduced inflammation, and restored joint homeostasis. This dual-pronged senotherapy offers a promising, non-surgical strategy for OA treatment and establishes a modular platform potentially applicable to other age-related diseases in the future.

sections.results:
Reliable model selection is critical for investigating the role of cellular senescence in OA. The ACLT model is widely employed due to its ability to replicate post-traumatic OA pathogenesis and induce both cartilage degeneration and chondrocyte senescence. Its standardized procedure, reproducibility, and consistent outcomes make it the preferred in vivo model for studying cartilage aging [ 3 , 20 ]. To validate the model, we assessed cartilage degradation and p16 INK4a expression in ACLT mice at various time points. Safranin O-Fast Green staining revealed progressive cartilage erosion, peaking at week 4, as quantified by Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) scores ( Fig. 2 A). This was accompanied by a time-dependent increase in p16 INK4a + chondrocytes, confirmed via immunofluorescence staining ( Fig. 2 B). The sham group at week 4 showed comparable levels to the baseline state at week 0 (ACLT) and significantly lower than the levels observed at 2 and 4 weeks post-ACLT surgery ( Fig. S1 ), which indicated the ACLT surgery can successfully induce OA-like pathology and chondrocyte senescence.

(B) Immunofluorescence images showing p16 INK4a expression in articular cartilage cryosections and quantification of p16 INK4a + cells (n = 3). Scale bars = 400 μm (overview), 200 μm (intermediate), 40 μm (high magnification). (C) Schematic workflow of DOX-induced senescence model in primary chondrocytes, including induction and validation steps. (D) SA-β-Gal staining of chondrocytes and quantification of SA-β-Gal + cells (n = 3). Scale bars = 100 μm. (E) Representative CLSM image showing co-localization of p16 INK4a (green) and DPP4 (red) in sCDs. Scale bar = 50 μm. (F) Flow cytometry analysis of p16 INK4a and DPP4 expression in chondrocytes, with corresponding quantitative data (n = 3). (G) Heatmap of relative mRNA expression levels of senescence- and OA-associated genes ( Cdkn2a, Cdkn1a, Dpp4, Il6, I l 1β, Tnfα, Mmp13, Mmp3, Col2a1, Aggrecan ) in chondrocytes (n = 3). (H) Western blotting analysis of DPP4, p16, p21, IL-6, and TNF-α expression in chondrocytes. (I) Quantification of IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β in cell culture supernatants by ELISA (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SD. ∗ P < 0.05, ∗∗ P < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗ P < 0.0001.

For in vitro studies, primary chondrocytes were harvested from articular cartilage of neonatal mice. The cells displayed typical round or polygonal morphology. Toluidine Blue O staining showed that the majority of cells exhibited a strong blue-purple positive reaction, indicating a high content of glycosaminoglycans in the cytoplasm ( Fig. S2 ). Immunofluorescence confirmed strong expression of collagen type II (COL-II), a chondrocyte-specific marker, verifying cellular identity ( Fig. S3 ). To induce senescence, we used doxorubicin (DOX), a classical chemotherapeutic agent known to intercalate DNA and block replication and transcription at subcytotoxic concentrations. This results in irreversible cell cycle arrest—a hallmark of cellular senescence—and provides a reliable platform for mechanistic studies and drug screening [ 21 , 22 ]. We established an in vitro chondrocyte senescence model using DOX and comprehensively characterized senescent features ( Fig. 2 C). SA-β-Gal staining showed a significant increase in positively stained cells in the DOX-treated group (84.1 ± 6.4 %) compared to controls (7.5 ± 2.6 %) ( Fig. 2 D). Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated strong co-localization of p16 INK4a and DPP4 in DOX-treated chondrocytes ( Fig. 2 E), corroborated by flow cytometry showing 39.1 ± 6.7 % double-positive cells ( Fig. 2 F), suggesting DPP4 as a potential surface marker for targeting sCDs. Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis indicated that DOX treatment significantly upregulated senescence-associated genes ( Cdkn2a, Cdk1a , Dpp4 ), SASP-related pro-inflammatory cytokines ( Il6 , Il1β , Tnfa ), and matrix-degrading enzymes ( Mmp13, Mmp3 ), while downregulating cartilage-specific genes ( Col2a1, Acan ) ( Fig. 2 G). Western blotting analysis confirmed that elevated levels of senescence markers (DPP4, p16 INK4a , p21) and SASP factors (IL-6, TNF-α) ( Fig. 2 H). Furthermore, DPP4 and p16 INK4a were also highly expressed in sCDs of humans ( Fig. S4 ), confirming the clinical relevance of the DPP4 target [ 23 ]. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) assays of the culture supernatant revealed a marked increase in IL-6 (6.7-fold), TNF-α (9.0-fold), and IL-1β (10.4-fold) compared to controls ( Fig. 2 I). In summary, we successfully established two complementary chondrocyte senescence models—an ACLT-induced in vivo and a DOX-induced in vitro—which serve as robust platforms for subsequent therapeutic evaluation.

Understanding the self-assembly mechanism of nanoparticles is essential for optimizing drug performance and enhancing stability. To identify the optimal assembly conditions, we systematically screened the molar ratios of BTZ and Sab. As shown in Fig. S5 , a 2:1 BTZ: Sab molar ratio (equivalent to a mass ratio of ∼1.1:1.0, mg/mg) of BTZ to Sab yielded monodisperse nanoparticles (BS) with a hydrodynamic diameter of 65.1 ± 2.1 nm and a low polydispersity index (PDI <0.2). Ratios deviating from this stoichiometry resulted in significant aggregation (diameter >100 nm, PDI >0.25), underscoring the importance of precise BTZ–Sab coordination for colloidal stability, which is consistent with previous findings [ 24 ]. Therefore, the 2:1 M ratio was adopted for subsequent experiments.

To elucidate the self-assembly mechanism, we assessed BS structural stability under various physicochemical conditions using UV–vis and fluorescence spectroscopy. Electrostatic interactions were evaluated by incubating BS in high-ionic-strength solutions (up to 2 M NaCl). The UV–vis spectra remained unchanged across all salt concentrations ( Fig. S6A ), suggesting that electrostatic forces are not the primary assembly driver. Next, the role of hydrophobic interactions was investigated. Upon exposure to sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), alterations in the BS absorption peak were observed ( Fig. S6B ), indicating that hydrophobic interactions contribute significantly to nanoparticle stabilization. To further probe coordination interactions between BTZ and Sab, we employed alizarin red S (ARS), a catechol-based dye that forms a yellow complex with BTZ, characterized by distinct UV–vis and fluorescence signals [ 24 ]. Increasing ARS: BTZ molar ratios caused a progressive redshift in the absorption band ( Fig. S6C ), confirming the successful complexation between ARS and BTZ. Upon addition of Sab to the ARS–BTZ complex, the spectrum resembled that of ARS alone ( Fig. S6D ), indicating that Sab disrupted the BTZ–ARS coordination. Fluorescence measurements further supported this conclusion. ARS–BTZ complexation significantly enhanced fluorescence at 560 nm ( Fig. S6E ), which was attenuated by Sab addition ( Fig. S6F ). Moreover, ARS underwent a visible color change upon complexation with BTZ (purple to yellow), which was reversed by Sab competition, restoring the original color ( Fig. S6G–H ). Furthermore, the FTIR results showed that the B-O stretching mode of the free BTZ at 1392 cm −1 was shifted to 1383 cm −1 in the BS NPs, and the phenolic hydroxyl of Sab at 3367 cm −1 was significantly diminished in the BS NPs, which is consistent with the results of the reported literature [ 25 , 26 ], confirming the formation of the borate ester bond between BTZ and Sab ( Fig. S7 ). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Sab competitively displaces ARS from BTZ, confirming that coordination interactions are the predominant driving force for BS nanoparticle self-assembly.

Carrier-free nanodrug delivery systems offer advantages such as high drug loading capacity and straightforward preparation, their limited aqueous stability and lack of targeting functionality constrain clinical translation. To address these issues, surface functionalization strategies have been explored [ 12 ]. Among them, modifying self-assembled nanodrugs with biomimetic cell membranes has become a prospective strategy to improve physiological stability and establish a platform for active targeting. Here, we engineered macrophage membrane-camouflaged nanoparticles (BS@M) and further modified them with anti-DPP4 antibodies to construct BS@MD. To achieve site-specific conjugation of the targeting antibody while preserving its bioactivity, we employed a metabolic glycoengineering strategy followed by copper-free click chemistry. This approach ensures that antibodies are anchored specifically to membrane protein residues rather than non-specifically to lipid domains. First, RAW 264.7 cells were incubated with Ac 4 ManNAz, a metabolic precursor that is incorporated into cell surface glycans, thereby introducing azide (N 3 ) groups as bioorthogonal handles onto the membrane. The biocompatibility test showed that 50 μM Ac 4 ManNAz is suitable for N 3 group incorporation ( Fig. S8 ). To validate N 3 expression via glycometabolic engineering, RAW 264.7 cells were pre-treated with 50 μM Ac 4 ManNAz and incubated with a DBCO-Cy5 probe. Fluorescence imaging revealed distinct red fluorescence in treated cells ( Fig. S9A ), and flow cytometry confirmed over 73 % surface labeling efficiency ( Fig. S9B ), confirming successful N 3 presentation. In parallel, anti-DPP4 antibodies were functionalized with dibenzocyclooctyne (DBCO) groups via a reaction between DBCO-PEG 4 -NHS ester and primary amines on the antibody [ 27 ]. To verify the successful synthesis of DBCO-modified antibodies, they were incubated with RAW-N 3 cells. Fluorescent secondary antibodies were employed to verify antibody grafting efficiency, and CLSM showed red fluorescence localized to RAW-N 3 cells only ( Fig. S10 ), confirming specific conjugation. Finally, the DBCO-modified antibodies were conjugated to the azide-presenting macrophage membranes (MM-N 3 ) coated BS nanoparticles, forming a stable triazole linkage (BS@MD). The synthesis schematic diagram was illustrated in Fig. 1 A.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) showed that both BS@M and BS@MD exhibited uniform spherical morphologies with visible membrane coatings, distinguishing them from uncoated BS cores ( Fig. 3 A). The hydrodynamic diameters measured via dynamic light scattering (DLS) indicated that of BS, BS@M, and BS@MD were 69.5 ± 1.6 nm, 79.9 ± 1.5 nm, and 82.1 ± 1.2 nm, respectively ( Fig. 3 B), consistent with macrophage membrane thickness [ 28 , 29 ]. Zeta potential measurements indicated a surface charge shift from −18.9 ± 2.8 mV (BS) to −28.6 ± 3.3 mV (BS@M) and −31.8 ± 1.1 mV (BS@MD) ( Fig. 3 C), confirming successful membrane and antibody modifications [ 30 ]. The colloidal stability of BS@MD was evaluated in PBS (pH 7.4) and complete cell culture medium (10 % FBS), demonstrating excellent stability over 7 days ( Fig. 3 D). Long-term stability assessment (4 °C, 28 days) also demonstrated that BS@MD could maintain its physicochemical properties ( Fig. S11 ). Moreover, the differences in preparation among different batches could be negligible ( Table S3 ). To confirm membrane coating, Dil-labeled macrophage membranes and FITC-labeled BS were co-extruded. Fluorescence microscopy revealed distinct co-localization signals ( Fig. 3 E), with Pearson’s correlation coefficient of 0.75 ± 0.03, demonstrating successful membrane encapsulation. The formation of the biomimetic core–shell structure is likely driven by hydrophobic interactions and electrostatic repulsion between the negatively charged BS cores and the cell membranes [ 31 ]. Coomassie blue-stained sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) analysis showed that the RAW 264.7 lane contains the most abundant protein bands, covering all the proteins of the entire cell. While the band patterns of BS@M were closely matched with MMs lane, both showing enrichment only in specific membrane protein band regions, confirming successful preservation of native membrane proteins in BS@M ( Fig. 3 F), which was consistent with previous reports [ 15 , 32 ]. Furthermore, antibody functionalization was verified by co-incubating BS@M and BS@MD with APC-labeled secondary antibodies (APC-IgG). Red fluorescence was detected only in the BS@MD group ( Fig. 3 G), indicating that the antibody had been successfully grafted. UV–vis spectra of various components are presented in Fig. S12 . Analysis of drug content via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) revealed BTZ and Sab loading levels of 5.65 % and 3.88 %, with encapsulation efficiencies of 68.2 % and 74.3 %, respectively ( Fig. S13 ). Given the acid sensitivity of borate ester bonds [ 33 ], the drug release kinetics of BS@MD was assessed at pH 7.4 (physiological) and pH 5.0 (lysosomal). Both BTZ and Sab exhibited synchronized release profiles. At pH 7.4, BS@MD showed minimal drug release (<10 % for both drugs over 24 h), while uncoated BS released over 23 %, highlighting the protective barrier function of the membrane. Under acidic conditions (pH 5.0), both BS and BS@MD achieved >70 % cumulative drug release ( Fig. 3 H), indicating that the membrane coating does not hinder the pH-responsive release properties of BS@MD [ 34 ]. To further simulate the pH release behavior of BS@MD in a real OA environment, we used simulated synovial fluid (SSF) as the release matrix and added a pH 6.0 condition to mimic the acidic milieu of inflamed synovium under OA conditions. The results showed that the various components in the SSF do not alter the inherent pH-responsive release mechanism of BS@MD. Due to protein adsorption and the increase in medium viscosity, the cumulative release rates of BTZ and Sab at all time points in SSF are generally lower than those in PBS at the same pH ( Fig. S14 ). The mechanism of pH-responsive cleavage of BS via breakage of catechol-boronate network is displayed in Fig. 3 I.

(B) Hydrodynamic diameter and PDI, (C) Zeta potential of BS, BS@M, and BS@MD (n = 3). (D) Colloid stability of BS@MD in PBS and DMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS at 37 °C over 7 days (n = 3). (E) Fluorescence microscope images showing co-localization of the BS core (FITC, green) and macrophage membranes (Dil, red), with Pearson’s correlation coefficient of 0.75 ± 0.03, confirming successful core–shell assembly. Scale bar = 4 μm (left), 2 μm (middle), 500 nm (right). (F) SDS-PAGE analysis comparing protein profiles of RAW 264.7 lysate, membrane vesicles (MMs), and BS@M (equal protein loading). (G) Fluorescence microscope images of BS@M and BS@MD following staining with APC-labeled secondary antibody (APC-IgG), verifying successful conjugation of anti-DPP4 antibodies via DBCO–azide click chemistry. Scale bar = 50 μm. (H) In vitro release profiles of BTZ and Sab from BS and BS@MD in PBS at pH 5.0 and 7.4 over 24 h. Data are presented as mean ± SD. (I) Mechanism of pH-responsive cleavage of BS via breakage of catechol-boronate network.

Pro-inflammatory mediators serve as a crucial link between cellular senescence and OA, with the SASP playing a central role. As core components of SASP, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β are major drivers of OA progression [ 35 , 36 ]. Their elevated expression in both ACLT-induced animal models and clinical OA samples correlates with disease severity and poor prognosis. Thus, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β were selected as representative SASP biomarkers to evaluate the neutralization capacity of BS@MD. Macrophage membrane-coated nanoparticles have demonstrated broad-spectrum capability in neutralizing pro-inflammatory mediators [ 32 , [37] , [38] , [39] ]. To verify this mechanism, we assessed the expression of cytokine receptors on macrophages via flow cytometry and western blotting. As expected for M1-polarized cells, LPS-primed macrophages exhibited significantly higher levels of TNFR1, IL-6Rα, and IL-1R1 compared to naïve controls ( Fig. 4 A). Western blotting corroborated the pattern of cytokine receptor upregulation ( Fig. 4 B). The co-culture experiment with immune cells showed that LPS-primed macrophage membranes (LPS-MM) and BS@MD did not cause activation of lymphocytes in the mouse spleen, indicating that LPS-MM and BS@MD do not trigger additional immune-inflammatory responses ( Fig. S15 ). To quantify the cytokine-neutralizing capacity of BS@MD, in vitro assays were performed with IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β at an initial concentration of 1 ng mL −1 ( Fig. 4 C). BS@MD at increasing concentrations (0–20 μg mL −1 ) was incubated with each cytokine at 37 °C for 30 min, followed by centrifugation (14,000× g , 10 min) to remove the nanoparticles. The supernatants were measured via ELISA and showed a dose-dependent cytokine neutralization kinetics, with BS@MD achieving maximum scavenging efficiencies of 35.7 % for IL-6, 24.3 % for TNF-α, and 31.5 % for IL-1β at 20 μg mL −1 ( Fig. 4 D). Fig. S16 further demonstrates that the outstanding pro-inflammatory factor neutralization ability of BS@MD is attributed to the two levels: the overexpressed receptors on the surface of macrophage membranes and the unique structure of the membrane-coated nanoparticles, which further increased the available surface area and stability of the cell membrane [ 40 ]. Considering that the complex intra-articular environment may have adverse effects on the membrane protein of BS@MD. We incubated BS@MD in 10 % FBS at 37 °C for 48 h, and then measured remaining TNFR1, IL-6Rα, and IL-1R1 on the membrane via western blotting. As shown in Fig. S17 , there is no significant reduction in the levels of three receptors on the BS@MD after the 48 h incubation compared to the control (0 h), confirming the stability of the macrophage membrane coating under physiologically relevant conditions.

BS@MD protects chondrocytes and macrophages from SASP-mediated paracrine effects in vitro. (B) Western blotting analysis of pro-inflammatory cytokine receptor expression in RAW 264.7 cells with or without LPS stimulation. (C) Schematic illustration depicting the neutralization of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β) by BS@MD. (D) Quantification of residual cytokines after incubation with increasing concentrations of BS@MD (0, 5, 10, and 20 μg mL −1 ) (n = 3). (E) Schematic diagram of the stimulation for nCDs and RAW 264.7 using the supernatant of sCDs (SCM), which was pretreated with BS@MD nanoparticles and removed by centrifugation before incubation. (F) RT-qPCR analysis of mRNA expression ( Cdkn2a, Cdkn1a, Col2a1, Mmp3, Mmp13, and Adamts5 ) and (G) Western blotting analysis (MMP13, MMP3, ADAMTS5, and COL-II) in nCDs incubated with different media (n = 3). Groups: (I 0 ): RAW; (II 0 ): RAW + SCM; (III 0 ): RAW + SCM pretreated with BS@MD. Scale bar = 50 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SD. ∗ P < 0.05, ∗∗ P < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗ P < 0.0001.

Chondrocytes, the only resident cells in articular cartilage, play a critical role in preserving cartilage homeostasis and ensuring proper joint function [ 41 , 42 ]. However, in OA, the accumulation of sCDs and their SASP secretion impair the activity of neighboring normal chondrocytes (nCDs), disrupting homeostasis and accelerating disease progression [ 43 ]. To evaluate whether BS@MD could mitigate SASP-mediated paracrine damage from sCDs to nCDs, we collected the supernatant from sCDs as senescent conditioned medium (SCM) and subsequently co-incubated it with BS@MD (5 μg mL −1 ) for 30 min. After ultracentrifugation, the supernatant was cultured with nCDs or RAW 264.7 cells for 24 h ( Fig. 4 E). qRT-PCR showed that the mRNA expression of two senescence markers ( p16 INK4a , p21 ) and three catabolic enzymes ( Mmp3 , Mmp13 , Adamts5 ) was significantly upregulated after induction by SCM compared to the control group. Conversely, the cartilage-specific gene Col2a1 was downregulated. Col2a1 encodes COL-II, a key ECM component vital for chondrocyte function and joint stability [ 44 ], while the catabolic enzymes degrade ECM, further compromising cartilage integrity [ 45 ]. Notably, BS@MD pretreatment partially reversed these effects—reducing expression of senescence and catabolic markers while restoring Col2a1 expression ( Fig. 4 F). Western blotting confirmed the same conclusion. BS@MD pretreatment reduced the protein expression levels of MMP3, MMP13, and ADAMTS5 in nCDs treated with SCM, while increasing the expression levels of COL-II ( Fig. 4 G). The DMMB assay also confirmed that nCDs cultured in SCM for 7 days secreted significantly fewer GAGs than those in normal medium, indicating the catabolic effect of SASP. Notably, pretreatment of SCM with BS@MD largely restored GAGs secretion to near-normal levels ( Fig. S18 ).

However, chondrocytes are not the only producers of SASP in joints. Fifty-five percent of cytokines come from synovial cells, with inflammatory macrophages as key contributors [ 46 ]. Macrophage polarization plays a pivotal role in regulating inflammation, with M1 macrophages promoting and M2 macrophages resolving inflammation. In OA, the transition from M1 to M2 is often impaired, leading to a heightened M1/M2 ratio in synovial tissues [ 46 , 47 ]. To investigate whether BS@MD can modulate macrophage polarization, flow cytometry was performed. BS@MD pretreatment reduced the proportion of CD86 + (M1) macrophages from 43.4 ± 0.3 % to 34.6 ± 1.1 % and increased CD206 + (M2) macrophages from 3.9 ± 1.3 % to 9.9 ± 1.3 % ( Fig. 4 H). Immunofluorescence staining yielded consistent results ( Fig. 4 I), indicating that BS@MD not only neutralizes SASP but also reprograms macrophage polarization to restore immune balance. In summary, BS@MD effectively protects both chondrocytes and macrophages from SASP-mediated paracrine damage by scavenging pro-inflammatory cytokines and modulating macrophage polarization.These findings highlight BS@MD’s therapeutic potential in mitigating OA pathogenesis.

To investigate the effects of BS@MD on macrophages, mRNA sequencing was performed on macrophages exposed to senescence-conditioned medium (SCM) with or without pretreated by BS@MD. Transcriptomic profiles between SCM and BS@MD groups were compared using differential expression gene (DEG) analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying macrophage reprogramming. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed clear transcriptional distinctions between the two groups ( Fig. 5 A). Close clustering of replicates within each group indicated high reproducibility, whereas clear separation between SCM and BS@MD groups reflected substantial transcriptomic differences. A Pearson correlation heatmap further confirmed inter-group divergence and intra-group consistency ( Fig. 5 B), with values closer to 1 indicating higher similarity in gene expression patterns. A Venn diagram illustrated 9898 genes co-expressed in both groups, with 845 and 906 genes uniquely expressed in the BS@MD and SCM groups, respectively ( Fig. 5 C). Volcano plots and heatmaps visualized the DEGs ( Fig. 5 D and E), identifying 6177 DEGs in the BS@MD group compared to SCM, with 2947 upregulated and 3230 downregulated. GO analysis categorized these DEGs into biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and molecular function (MF) terms ( Fig. 5 F). Notably, processes such as regulation of innate immune response, cytokine receptor binding, and cytokine activity were suppressed. KEGG pathway analysis indicated significant alterations in inflammation-related pathways, including the TNF signaling pathway, NOD-like receptor signaling pathway, and NF-κB signaling pathway ( Fig. 5 G). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) further confirmed significant downregulation of these pathways ( Fig. 5 H). Western blot ( Fig. 5 I) and qPCR analysis ( Fig. 5 J) also validated that BS@MD pretreatment reduced the expression of p-NF-κB p65, NLRP3, TNF-α, and IL-1β compared to the SCM group. Together, these findings suggest that BS@MD modulates macrophage polarization homeostasis by suppressing inflammatory factor expression via the NF-κB signaling pathway.

(D) Volcano plot and (E) heatmap showed DEGs in BS@MD and SCM groups. (F) Top 30 down-regulated differential GO enrichment pathways and (G) top 20 KEGG enrichment of DEGs after treatment with BS@MD compared to SCM. (H) GSEA enrichment analysis of NF-κB signaling pathway, NOD-like receptor signaling pathway, and TNF signaling pathway. Data are presented as mean ± SD. ∗ P < 0.05, ∗∗ P < 0.01, ∗∗∗∗ P < 0.0001.

Precise targeting of sCDs is critical to enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of OA treatments. To evaluate the targeting capability of BS@MD, we labeled BS@M and BS@MD with Cy5 and evaluated their uptake in nCDs and sCDs using Hoechst 33342 for nuclear visualization. After 2 h of incubation, BS@MD showed minimal red fluorescence in nCDs, whereas intense perinuclear fluorescence was observed in sCDs. In contrast, BS@M displayed diffuse and nonspecific cytoplasmic distribution in both cell types ( Fig. 6 A). Flow cytometry further confirmed the selective uptake of BS@MD: internalization was significantly higher in sCDs (58.3 %) compared to nCDs (12.0 %), reflecting a 4.86-fold increase ( Fig. 6 B). This trend was also verified on human sCDs ( Fig. S19 ). Flow cytometry indicated that the targeting efficiency of BS@MD for H-sCDs was up to 76.7 %. To further confirm that the targeting specificity of BS@MD is attributed to anti-DPP4 antibody grafting, sCDs were pre-incubated with an excess of free anti-DPP4 antibody (10 μg mL −1 ) for 1 h to saturate all DPP4 epitopes on the cell surface. Then they were incubated with Cy5-labeled BS@MD for 2 h. CLSM results showed that sCDs treated with anti-DPP4 antibody significantly reduced the uptake of BS@MD compared with the sCDs ( Fig. S20A ). Flow cytometry results also showed that the uptake efficiency decreased by 92 % ( Fig. S20B ). It is fully demonstrated that the anti-DPP4 antibody is the key factor to endow the BS@MD with specificity for targeting sCDs. DPP4, also known as CD26, is an enzyme involved in immune regulation and metabolic inflammation. This protein is well-documented to be overexpressed on the surface of senescent cells [ 16 , [48] , [49] , [50] ]. Antibody–receptor binding facilitates targeted internalization of nanoparticles, making anti-DPP4 antibody a rational design choice for selective delivery to sCDs. To investigate the intracellular fate of BS@MD, we used LysoTracker Green to label lysosomes. Co-localization with Cy5-labeled BS@MD indicated lysosomal entrapment, as shown by overlapping fluorescence and pixel intensity profiles ( Fig. 6 C). Consequently, this result supports a lysosome-dependent, acid-triggered drug release mechanism for BS@MD.

Intra-articular injection is a common strategy to enhance drug bioavailability in joint tissues. However, challenges such as rapid drug clearance and poor tissue penetration limit its efficacy. To determine whether BS@MD enhances joint retention via targeted delivery, we administered Cy5.5-labeled BS, BS@M, and BS@MD into the knee joints of OA mice 4 weeks post-ACLT surgery. Fluorescence imaging (IVIS Spectrum) was performed at 2, 24, 48, and 72 h post-injection. The fluorescence signals in the BS and BS@M groups declined sharply over time, while the BS@MD group maintained strong fluorescence ( Fig. 6 D). At 72 h, the retention rates in the joints were 41.4 % for BS, 52.8 % for BS@M, and 94.8 % for BS@MD ( Fig. 6 E), demonstrating the superior joint-retention capability of BS@MD. After 72 h, the main organs of OA mice were extracted for fluorescence intensity analysis. Ex vivo imaging revealed high fluorescence accumulation in the joint tissue, second only to the liver ( Fig. 6 F). Fluorescence quantitative analysis revealed that the BS@MD group was 1.4- and 1.9-fold greater than that observed in the BS@M and BS groups, respectively ( Fig. 6 G), consistent with in vivo findings. Subsequently, inflamed joints were sectioned and subjected to immunofluorescence staining. Compared with the BS@M group, the BS@MD group showed red fluorescent particles (Cy5.5) localized predominantly within green p16 INK4a + sCDs (FITC) ( Fig. 6 H).This is mainly attributed to three key reasons. Firstly, the progression of OA leads to a decrease in proteoglycan content, reducing the charge on the joint surface and thereby minimizing the electrostatic repulsion against BS@MD [ 51 ]. Secondly, the degradation and structural disorder of the superficial matrix significantly increase its permeability [ 52 ], allowing BS@MD to bypass the damaged superficial zone and subsequently accumulate in the more loosely structured deep zone. Lastly, and most importantly, the precise targeting of sCDs by BS@MD enables it to remain in cells for a longer period, increasing the drug concentration within the joint. Furthermore, considering the heterogeneity of the joint microenvironment, other cell types within the joint, such as synoviocytes, may also undergo senescence and highly express DPP4. Therefore, we further evaluated the localization of BS@MD in synovial tissues. Immunofluorescence images also showed that BS@MD was mainly located in p16 INK4a + synoviocytes ( Fig. S21 ). This surprise could potentially offer additional benefits by mitigating synovitis and further confirms the specificity of “DPP4-targeting”. Collectively, these results highlight two key mechanisms underlying the enhanced targeting and retention of BS@MD: (1) Anti-DPP4 antibody-mediated recognition and internalization into sCDs [ 17 ]; and (2) the macrophage membrane coating. The macrophage membrane, derived from the host’s own immune cells, displays “self-marker” proteins (e.g., CD47) that confer effective immune evasion by CD47–SIRPα signaling to minimize opsonization and phagocytic clearance [ 53 ]. This property is crucial for prolonging the nanoparticle’s circulation time, providing it with more opportunities to accumulate within the inflamed joint. Coupled with the innate inflammatory tropism of the macrophage membrane, these features enable BS@MD to selectively accumulate in senescent and inflamed joint regions, thereby improving therapeutic potential in OA.

Senescent cells are characterized by resistance to apoptosis and persistent secretion of SASP. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of our formulations, we systematically assessed their ability to induce apoptosis and suppress SASP in sCDs. Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assays revealed that BS@MD induced sCDs death in a dose-dependent manner. In contrast, significant cytotoxicity toward nCDs was observed only at concentrations exceeding 5 μg mL −1 (cell viability <90 %) ( Fig. S22 ). This trend is also reflected in human chondrocytes ( Fig. S23 ), further demonstrating the clinical relevance of the current experiment. Thus, 5 μg mL −1 was chosen as the optimal concentration for BS@MD in subsequent studies, and other formulations were adjusted accordingly based on drug loading. Under these conditions, BS exhibited strong cytotoxicity toward both nCDs and sCDs due to its non-selective action. In contrast, BS@MD showed pronounced cytotoxicity specifically against sCDs but minimal effects on nCDs, attributable to its superior targeting capability that mediated ∼5-fold higher uptake in sCDs compared with nCDs ( Fig. 6 B). BS@M displayed reduced cytotoxicity overall, as the macrophage membrane coating delayed drug release and lacked active targeting [ 31 ], leading to lower toxicity in both sCDs (compared with BS@MD) and nCDs (compared with BS). The BTZ, Sab, and BS groups exhibited similar cytotoxicity profiles in both sCDs and nCDs, highlighting their lack of target specificity ( Fig. 7 A). Once internalized, the acidic lysosomal environment triggers the rapid release of the payload from the BS@MD core ( Fig. 3 H), resulting in a high local drug concentration that effectively induces apoptosis. Live/dead cell staining further supported these findings. The BS@MD group exhibited the most intense red fluorescence, with the highest dead/live cell ratio (2.53-fold) among all groups ( Fig. 7 B). Flow cytometry showed that all formulations significantly induced apoptosis in sCDs, with BS@MD demonstrating the strongest efficacy—1.24-fold and 1.66-fold greater than BTZ and Sab alone, respectively ( Fig. 7 C). This enhanced efficacy is attributed to its superior targeting capability to sCDs and the synergistic pro-apoptotic effects of BTZ and Sab [ 24 ]. Representative SA-β-gal staining visualized sCDs clearance, with the PBS group showing extensive blue staining (71.6 % SA-β-gal + cells) and the BS@MD group exhibiting significantly reduced (19.8 % SA-β-gal + cells) ( Fig. 7 D). We further assessed the SASP levels in cell supernatants. ELISA results indicated that BS@MD significantly reduced levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β to 36.3 %, 31.9 %, and 18.0 % of those in the PBS group, respectively ( Fig. 7 E).

At the mechanistic level, the BCL-2 family is a pivotal regulator of apoptosis and constitutes a critical target for senolytic therapy [ 7 , 54 ]. Pro-apoptotic members, such as BAX and BAK, induce apoptosis by forming pores in the mitochondrial outer membrane, thereby promoting the release of cytotoxic molecules and activation of caspases. In contrast, anti-apoptotic proteins like BCL-2 prevent this process by binding to the BH3 domains of BAX and BAK, effectively blocking mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) [ 55 ]. Thus, numerous researchers have designed BH3 mimetics to block BCL-2 proteins, mediating the clearance of senescent cells [ 56 , 57 ]. Among them, as a BH3 mimetic with pan-BCL-2 inhibitory activity, Sab is widely used to induce cell apoptosis [ 19 ]. Additionally, the NF-κB pathway serves as a central regulator of SASP, governing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors [ 6 , 9 ]. Suppression of NF-κB activity can effectively attenuate SASP levels and alleviate the inflammatory burden, thereby improving OA microenvironment [ 58 ]. As the first proteasome inhibitor approved by the FDA, BTZ has exhibited promising activity in clinical tumor treatment and more recently in OA due to its potent NF-κB inhibitory activity [ 59 , 60 ]. To verify whether the reduction of sCDs and SASP aligns with our system’s design—synergistic inhibition of BCL-2 and NF-κB pathways by Sab and BTZ, the western blotting analysis was performed. BS@MD treatment significantly decreased BCL-2 expression while upregulating Bak, Bax, and cleaved caspase-3, confirming activation of the apoptotic pathway. BTZ-containing formulations also markedly reduced the expression of p-NF-κB p65 and p-IκBα, suggesting an effective inhibition of the NF-κB pathway and providing a rational explanation for the reduced expression of pro-inflammatory and pro-survival genes ( Fig. 7 F). In summary, these results demonstrate that BS@MD can precisely target sCDs and release BTZ and Sab in response to lysosomal acidic pH, thereby synergistically inhibiting the BCL-2 and NF-κB pathways to induce sCDs apoptosis while significantly reducing SASP secretion ( Fig. 7 G).

To assess the in vivo therapeutic efficacy of BS@MD in OA, we employed the ACLT mouse model. The experimental workflow is schematically illustrated in Fig. 8 A. Considering ACLT surgery is a highly aggressive model designed to rapidly and reliably induce a severe OA phenotype, 8 weeks after ACLT surgery is usually regarded as a common time point for evaluating the repair of joint injuries [ 61 ]. The body weight of mice in all treatment groups consistently increased, and the body weight at various time points was comparable to that of the sham group ( Fig. 8 B), indicating no overt systemic toxicity from any formulation. To assess systemic inflammatory responses, we quantified serum SASP-related cytokines of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α in ACLT mice at 8 weeks post-surgery. These pro-inflammatory factors are known to increase in OA and correlate with disease severity [ 62 ]. Compared to the PBS group, BTZ treatment moderately reduced cytokine levels, while BS@M and especially BS@MD elicited more pronounced reductions ( Fig. 8 C), suggesting enhanced systemic anti-inflammatory effects.

Subchondral bone degradation is a key pathological hallmark of OA. We used micro-computed tomography (Micro-CT) to assess the osteophyte formation and subchondral bone remodeling. At 8 weeks post-surgery, the PBS-treated ACLT mice displayed prominent osteophyte development (highlighted by red boxes), severe cartilage/subchondral erosion, and surface pitting. In contrast, BS@M treatment substantially reduced osteophyte formation, whereas BS@MD achieved the most effective suppression ( Fig. 8 D). Subchondral bone microstructural changes were further assessed by measuring bone volume fraction (BV/TV), trabecular thickness (Tb. Th), trabecular number (Tb. N), and trabecular separation (Tb. Sp) across all groups. Compared to the sham group, the ACLT-mice exhibited significantly increased BV/TV, Tb. N, and Tb. Th, along with decreased Tb. Sp, consistent with subchondral bone sclerosis. Treatments with PBS, Sab, or BS did not improve these parameters, and Sab’s pro-apoptotic effects even appeared to exacerbate cartilage damage. BTZ conferred moderate structural protection, potentially due to a reduced inflammatory burden through inhibition of the NF-κB pathway. However, BS@M significantly attenuated subchondral bone sclerosis by reducing BV/TV, Tb. N, and Tb. Th, while increasing Tb. Sp. BS@MD achieved the most pronounced restoration, with all microstructural parameters approaching those of the sham group ( Fig. 8 E). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that BS@MD effectively mitigates OA progression by reducing systemic inflammation, suppressing osteophyte formation, and reversing subchondral bone sclerosis.

We subsequently conducted a histological evaluation of the cartilage tissue, which included hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining, Safranin O-Fast Green staining, toluidine blue staining, and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining. As expected, the ACLT groups exhibited pronounced cartilage degeneration, characterized by chondrocyte loss, uneven surface, and ECM degradation. In contrast, the Sham group maintained well-organized cartilage architecture and a smooth articular surface. Remarkably, BS@MD treatment preserved cartilage structure and cellular morphology to a degree closely resembling that of the Sham group ( Fig. 9 A). Safranin O-Fast Green and Toluidine blue staining further confirmed the extent of cartilage injury. The ACLT group exhibited marked reductions and heterogeneous distribution of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), indicative of ECM breakdown. In contrast, BS@MD treatment restored GAGs deposition to levels comparable to the Sham-operated mice ( Fig. 9 B and C). Furthermore, according to the OARSI ( Fig. 9 D) and modified Mankin scoring system ( Fig. 9 E), the BS@MD group exhibited the lowest score, except for the Sham-operated group, indicating the most effective treatment outcome. Morphometric analysis revealed that BS@MD-treated joints maintained cartilage thickness comparable to the Sham group ( Fig. 9 F), with minimal histological signs of degradation ( Fig. 9 G), confirming its ability to effectively prevent structural cartilage damage. To investigate the senescence-related inflammatory microenvironment, we performed IHC staining for p16 INK4a , IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α. The Sham group exhibited low expression of p16 INK4a and SASP-related cytokines, indicative of a non-senescent, anti-inflammatory tissue environment. Conversely, ACLT-mice exhibited marked upregulated of p16 INK4a and SASP-related cytokines, confirming a senescence-driven inflammatory state. However, BS@MD treatment significantly downregulated these markers, reducing p16 INK4a + cells and SASP components. While BTZ and BS@M also showed partial efficacy, other treatments did not produce notable effects ( Fig. 9 H).

Synovial inflammation is a hallmark of OA and a critical factor influencing disease progression and prognosis [ 63 ]. H&E staining of synovial tissues demonstrated that treatment with BS@MD markedly reduced synovial inflammation, characterized by a thin intimal lining (1–3 cell layers) and a sparsely cellular subintimal region, with the lowest synovitis score among all treatment groups. In contrast, other groups showed varying degrees of synovial lining thickening, increased infiltration of inflammatory cells, and pannus formation, with the PBS and Sab groups being the most severe, indicating that BS@MD treatment effectively alleviated synovial inflammation ( Fig. S24A ). Macrophage polarization within the synovium plays a pivotal role in OA pathogenesis and resolution. To assess the immunomodulatory effect of BS@MD, we evaluated the M1 (CD86 + ) and M2 (CD206 + ) phenotypic markers in synovial tissues. BS@MD treatment significantly increased the proportion of CD206 + (green) macrophages while reducing the presence of CD86 + (red) macrophages, indicating a shift toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. In contrast, the PBS group showed predominant M1 polarization, with higher numbers of CD86 + cells and fewer CD206 + cells ( Fig. S24B ). To further confirm the macrophage reprogramming effect of BS@MD at the transcriptional level in vivo, CD11b + cells (monocyte/macrophage) were sorted in the synovial tissue after BS@MD treatment and analyzed for the expression of classic M1 and M2 marker genes by qPCR. Consistent with the results of the immunofluorescence, BS@MD treatment significantly downregulated the mRNA levels of M1 markers ( Nos2 , Il1β ) and upregulated those of M2 markers ( Arg1 , Mrc1 ) compared to the PBS control ( Fig. S25 ). These results indicate that BS@MD effectively regulates synovial macrophage polarization, highlighting its therapeutic potential in OA management.

To further validate the therapeutic efficacy of BS@MD in a physiologically relevant model of OA, we employed a naturally aged OA mouse model. 20-month-old mice were compared with 2-month-old young controls to assess spontaneous OA progression and the therapeutic effect of BS@MD. The aged mice received intra-articular injections of either BS@MD or PBS twice a week for a month. Histological examination through H&E, Safranin O-Fast Green, and Toluidine Blue staining ( Fig. S26 A-C ) revealed pronounced cartilage destruction, proteoglycan loss, and surface erosion in the 20-month-old PBS-treated group compared to the young controls. In contrast, BS@MD-treated aged mice exhibited significantly preserved cartilage integrity, with smoother articular surfaces, reduced fibrillation, and maintained proteoglycan content, as quantified by lower OARSI scores and cartilage degradation score, but thicker cartilage ( Fig. S26 D-F ). IHC analysis further demonstrated that the articular cartilage of aged control mice showed strong positivity for the senescence marker p16 INK4a and the SASP-related cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α. However, BS@MD treatment markedly reduced the expression of all these markers, indicating simultaneous attenuation of both cellular senescence and inflammatory burden in the joint tissue ( Fig. S27 ). Collectively, these results demonstrate that BS@MD effectively mitigates OA progression in a naturally aged mouse model by preserving cartilage structure and reducing the senescence-associated inflammatory microenvironment, thereby providing robust evidence for its therapeutic potential in age-related OA.

To assess the in vivo biosafety of the various formulations, whole blood and major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) were collected for subsequent analysis. Routine hematological analyses were performed to measure leukocytes, lymphocytes, intermediate cells, and granulocytes. All values remained within normal physiological ranges, indicating no hematological abnormalities ( Fig. S28A ). Hepatic and renal functions were evaluated through standard serum biomarkers, including glutamic-pyruvic transaminase (ALT), glutamic-oxalacetic transaminase (AST), urine acid (UA), creatinine (CREA), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). No statistically significant differences were observed among the seven experimental groups, suggesting preserved liver and kidney function ( Fig. S28B ). Additionally, H&E staining demonstrated no obvious pathological changes in any major organs ( Fig. S29 ), further supporting the absence of systemic toxicity. To further evaluate the dose-toxicity window of BS@MD, we increased the concentration of BS@MD to 1.0 or 1.5 mg kg −1 and administered it for one month. Similarly, no obvious pathological changes in the major organs were observed ( Fig. S30 ). Moreover, the immunogenicity test also demonstrated that repeated administration of BS@MD in the joints of mice did not lead to the production of anti-PEG ( Fig. S31 ) or any other antibodies against the components of BS@MD (including anti-membrane-protein and anti-DPP4 antibodies), as the performance of BS@MD after co-incubation with the therapeutic mouse serum (after 4 injections of BS@MD) was not affected ( Fig. S32 ). Taken together, these comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that BS@MD exhibits excellent biocompatibility and does not elicit hematological, hepatic, or renal toxicity in vivo.

Although BS@MD demonstrated favourable efficacy in this study, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the in vivo molecular mechanisms after BS@MD treatment remain incompletely characterized. More comprehensive studies, including transcriptomic and proteomic analyses, are required to map the remodeling of the cartilage and synovial immune microenvironment. Second, detailed pharmacokinetic and biodistribution investigations in ex vivo and in vivo large-animal models (e.g., porcine) are essential before clinical translation. Finally, considering the benefits and limitations of current OA treatments such as hyaluronic acid and corticosteroids, combination strategies are a promising direction. For instance, BS@MD could be incorporated into HA-based delivery systems or used together with corticosteroids to provide rapid pain relief while simultaneously exerting anti-inflammatory and senomorphic effects. Collectively, these efforts will further refine the therapeutic potential of BS@MD for translational application in OA.

sections.conclusion: This study presents a promising dual-pronged OA therapeutic strategy aimed at clearing sCDs and providing broad-spectrum neutralization of SASP. We developed engineered macrophage membrane-coated BS self-assembled nanoparticles that are functionalized with the anti-DPP4 antibody, referred to as BS@MD. First, these nanovesicles function as “biomimetic nanosponges” that broadly neutralize SASP (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β) in the OA microenvironment. This action relieves chondrocyte senescence by minimizing SASP-mediated paracrine damage and reprogramming macrophage polarization toward a reparative M2 phenotype, thereby maintaining microenvironmental homeostasis. Meanwhile, the anti-DPP4 modification confers BS@MD with precise targeting capability toward sCDs while sparing nCDs. Once internalized, the acidic lysosomal environment triggers controlled release of BTZ and Sab, leading to coordinated inhibition of the BCL-2 and NF-κB signaling pathways. This action promotes apoptosis in sCDs and effectively suppresses the production of the SASP. In conclusion, BS@MD significantly attenuates both cellular senescence and SASP-driven inflammation, resulting in preserved cartilage integrity, reduced synovitis, and improved subchondral bone architecture in vivo. While further investigations are required to clarify the underlying mechanisms in greater detail, our work offers a compelling strategy for OA intervention by simultaneously targeting both the root causes and symptomatic manifestations of the disease, which holds promise for the treatment of other age-associated degenerative disorders in the future.
